medical.title: Early-stage breast cancer gains first newly approved hormone therapy in more than 20 years
medical.summary: For the first time in more than two decades, the FDA has approved a new hormone therapy for early-stage breast cancer, marking a monumental shift in how the most common form of the disease is treated.

medical.title: Drones could soon fly blood, defibrillators and medicine to patients
medical.summary: Paramedics in one Florida county may soon be able to call in a drone to bring blood to a patient who's bleeding heavily.

medical.title: Disrupting a developing brain circuit in adolescence may have lasting social effects
medical.summary: Adolescence is often described as a turbulent period of life marked by growing independence, changing social relationships and unpredictable shifts in behavior. According to researchers, tweens' and teens' behavioral changes reflect a brain that is still actively developing, yet scientists know surprisingly little about the neural mechanisms that shape social behavior during this critical stage of life.

medical.title: England shows widest socioeconomic gap in frailty among 31 countries
medical.summary: Older adults from disadvantaged socioeconomic backgrounds experience greater levels of frailty, with England showing the biggest gap between socioeconomic groups among the 31 countries studied.

medical.title: Prior authorization limits help expand opioid addiction treatment where approvals were a frequent roadblock, study finds
medical.summary: State laws limiting prior authorization requirements for opioid use disorder medications were associated with increased buprenorphine use in Medicaid, but only in states where those requirements were frequent barriers to access, according to a new study led by University of Michigan researchers.

medical.title: FDA approves bezuclastinib in combination with sunitinib as new second-line therapy for patients with GIST
medical.summary: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved a combination of bezuclastinib plus sunitinib as second-line therapy after first-line treatment with imatinib for adults with advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) based on evidence from the phase 3 PEAK study led by Dana-Farber Cancer Institute showing that the combination outperformed standard therapy with sunitinib alone.

medical.title: Reducing or quitting smoking linked to lower risk for developing psoriasis
medical.summary: Smoking reduction is associated with a reduced risk for developing psoriasis, including psoriasis vulgaris (PsV) and palmoplantar pustulosis (PPP), according to a research letter published online Nov. 18 in JAMA Dermatology.

medical.title: FDA approves Nelkarmi for ALK-positive non-small cell lung cancer
medical.summary: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has granted approval to Nelkarmi (neladalkib), a kinase inhibitor, for adults with locally advanced or metastatic anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK)-positive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who were previously treated. The approval was granted to Nuvalent and GSK.

medical.title: Common patterns of b/tsDMARD use identified in rheumatoid arthritis
medical.summary: Common patterns of biologic and targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (b/tsDMARD) use are seen among patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), and these patterns are associated with underlying genetic associations, according to a study published online Nov. 20 in Arthritis & Rheumatology.

medical.title: How methylmercury impairs forebrain inhibitory circuits and induces abnormal behavior in mice
medical.summary: Global efforts have sought to reduce mercury pollution, but methylmercury (MeHg) remains a persistent environmental hazard that bioaccumulates in aquatic food chains. Humans are exposed to MeHg primarily through contaminated seafood. Minamata disease, officially recognized in Japan in 1956, demonstrated the devastating neurological consequences of MeHg poisoning. Since then, researchers have investigated its neurotoxic effects, including sensory, motor and psychiatric symptoms. Despite clinical reports of behavioral disturbances in people affected by MeHg poisoning, the neural circuits underlying these abnormalities remain poorly understood.

medical.title: HIV viral control is necessary but not sufficient for healthy aging
medical.summary: Individuals with HIV show signs of faster biological aging compared with people without HIV. In other words, indicators of bodily functions that can be measured in the blood appear more like those of an older individual than those of someone the same age.

medical.title: Doctors report less burnout in practices they rate as efficient, even during long workweeks
medical.summary: When it comes to physician burnout, how you spend your working hours may matter more than how many hours you work.

medical.title: Novel metric accurately distinguishes metastasis from an independent primary tumor
medical.summary: Research has found that the newly developed Clonal Relatedness Index (CRI) can accurately determine whether tumors in the same patient share a common clonal origin. The findings, detailed in an article appearing in The Journal of Molecular Diagnostics, have important implications for the clinical management of complex cases of cancers of the digestive system and abdominal lining, specifically gastrointestinal, hepatopancreatobiliary and peritoneal carcinomas.

medical.title: Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle
medical.summary: Researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a compound that could transform weight-loss treatment by helping the body burn more energy instead of suppressing appetite like Ozempic and Wegovy. In mice, the compound boosted energy expenditure by up to 18%, improved blood sugar control, reduced liver fat, and promoted weight loss without significant muscle loss. Even more promising, combining it with existing GLP-1 medications produced greater benefits than either treatment alone.

science.title: New EU Bureaucracy Index: EU law has more than doubled since 2010
science.summary: The new EU Bureaucracy Index measures the volume of EU law in force, and it shows a record high: At the end of 2025, the EU regulations and directives in force comprised around 47,600 standard pages, 118% more than in 2010. The volume of EU law has thus more than doubled in 15 years, and it continued to grow in 2025. The main drivers are sanctions regulations and new sets of rules in environmental, consumer and health law.

science.title: A star's 'obliquity' likely has little impact on a given planet's habitability
science.summary: A star's axial tilt as it relates to the circumstellar disk that surrounds it is known as stellar obliquity. Over space and time, there are a myriad of solar-type stars with all sorts of obliquities. But the question heretofore has always been what effect a given star's initial obliquity has on the planetary system that forms around it.

science.title: What draws data centers to a community?
science.summary: As Oklahoma communities weigh new data center development, research co-authored by a University of Oklahoma architecture professor offers insight into what draws major technology companies to locations—and why those choices matter locally.

science.title: Hurricane season wrap-up: El Niño fueled record number of Pacific storms but calmed Atlantic
science.summary: The 2026 hurricane season, which officially ends on Nov. 30, will be remembered as a year of contrasts between the Atlantic and Pacific, a classic indication of a hurricane season influenced by a very strong El Niño. Below-normal activity across the Atlantic basin was offset by above-average activity in the Pacific, including two disasters in Hawaii.

science.title: Ultrathin 'rainbow' sails could power spacecraft and shade the Earth
science.summary: For years, whimsically minded space enthusiasts have been dreaming of sailing across the vastness of the void on beams of sunlight. Photons, the massless particles that make up those beams of sunlight, still carry momentum and can therefore impart a gentle push when they bounce off a surface. This force is the concept behind "solar sailing," which has been having a bit of a moment in the last decade as several proof-of-concept flights have shown it is indeed feasible.

science.title: How alfalfa forms root nodules without rhizobia
science.summary: A research team led by professor Feng Jian at the Institute of Genetics and Developmental Biology (IGDB) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences has uncovered a cytokinin–NODULE INCEPTION (NIN) regulatory module associated with spontaneous root nodule formation in alfalfa (Medicago sativa).

science.title: New chemical route delivers first synthesis of plant compound with cough-suppressing potential
science.summary: Neotuberostemonine, a complex plant-derived alkaloid with promising antitussive activity, has remained a challenging target for chemical synthesis for nearly 30 years. Researchers have now achieved its first total synthesis, alongside the synthesis of neostenine and the putative structure of tuberostemonine L. The findings also reveal how the nearly planar geometry of nitrogen atoms contributes to the oxidative instability of these alkaloids, offering new insights and synthetic strategies for natural-product chemistry and future drug discovery.

science.title: Laser light reveals where electrons accumulate in atomically thin semiconductor stacks
science.summary: Stacking semiconductors—the chips that power phones, computers and so much more—enables quicker signal movement with less energy, but how does the process actually work? Turns out shining a literal light on the semiconducting materials can help elucidate how the electrons move in the stack, according to a multi-institutional team in Japan. The approach could help inform the development of more efficient, low-power electronics, the researchers said.

science.title: Underwater robots reveal first salp species known to live exclusively in deep sea
science.summary: Salps are barrel-shaped gelatinous animals that play an important role in ocean ecosystems. More than 20 years ago, researchers observed an unfamiliar salp in the deep waters of Monterey Bay. Using specimens and data collected by MBARI's advanced underwater robots, Larry Madin, deputy director emeritus at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution and an MBARI adjunct, recently published a detailed description of the glass salp (Vitreosalpa gemini) in the journal Marine Biodiversity. This striking species is the first salp known to live exclusively in the deep sea.

science.title: New workflow advances programmable chromosome editing in plants
science.summary: A study published in Nature Protocols on Nov. 17 presents a detailed experimental workflow for programmable chromosome manipulation in plants. The platform was developed by a research group led by Gao Caixia at the Institute of Genetics and Developmental Biology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

science.title: Catalysts come alive—electron microscopy reveals the secret dynamic life of nanoparticles
science.summary: University of Nottingham researchers have uncovered hidden nanoscale transformations that could help design cleaner fuels and more efficient catalysts.

science.title: Mitochondria rebranding: Goodbye, powerhouse of the cell. Hello, lungs of the cell?
science.summary: If you remember one thing from high school biology, there's a good chance it's this: Mitochondria are the powerhouse of the cell.

science.title: Local protein supply chain keeps nerve cells' mitochondria in check
science.summary: Some tracers used in hospital scans to check what is happening inside a patient's body are so short-lived they must be made on demand on site or rushed in by courier. A new study led by Angelika Harbauer's group at the Max Planck Institute for Biological Intelligence shows that nerve cells use similar strategies to deliver a protein that checks for damage in their mitochondria, the tiny structures that supply energy, balance calcium levels and perform other vital tasks.

science.title: Sex in Britain has changed significantly, especially among young people
science.summary: The sex lives of people in Britain have shifted markedly since 1990, and their sexual and reproductive health needs are substantial and varied, according to the fourth National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal-4). The first five papers from the survey—one of the largest studies of sexual behavior in the world—are published in The Lancet.

science.title: Microplastics in nearly 8 in 10 fish sampled off Oman's Sohar coast
science.summary: Researchers at Sultan Qaboos University detected microplastics in the gills or digestive tracts of 95 of 120 fish sampled off Sohar in the Sea of Oman. Published in Scientific Reports, the study provides a baseline for tracking microplastic pollution in fish along this stretch of Oman's coast.

science.title: Blind sample test reveals how BepiColombo could decode Mercury's mineral makeup
science.summary: An international team of researchers, including scientists from Planetary Science Institute (PSI), has demonstrated that instruments aboard the BepiColombo spacecraft can operate together to identify the minerals that make up Mercury's surface, addressing a longstanding challenge in planetary science. The findings, published in Planetary and Space Science, come as the joint European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) mission entered orbit around Mercury this week.

science.title: Carbon-rich soil near old oaks does not attract more earthworms, study finds
science.summary: Solitary oaks in traditional Romanian wood pastures create islands of carbon-rich soil around their trunks. However, a research team led by the Universities of Göttingen and Hildesheim found this does not mean more earthworms. In traditional wood pastures in Romania, the topsoil near the trunk held about a third more organic carbon and a quarter more nitrogen than the open grassland, yet earthworm numbers were no higher. As such trees decline across Europe, it is important to understand what they contribute to the soil. The results were published in the journal Agroforestry Systems.

science.title: Self-assembling nanocarriers show promise for delivering CRISPR to tumors and slowing growth
science.summary: A self-assembling supramolecular nanocarrier protects Cas9 RNPs from degradation, enhances systemic delivery and preferential tumor accumulation, and enables pH-responsive intracellular release. Developed by researchers at the Institute of Science Tokyo, this platform achieved a 37.2% indel frequency at the luciferase target locus in HeLa-Luc tumor tissue in mice, compared with 1.5% with free RNPs, and suppressed tumor growth in separate mouse models. These findings support the further development of systemic CRISPR-based cancer therapies.

science.title: Quantum blueprint maps a practical path to testing unusual entanglement
science.summary: Adrian Del Maestro knows how to engineer a quantum fingerprint. Rick Mukherjee has a gift for tuning atoms. Their combined expertise has taken a theory sketched out on paper and created a pathway for real experiments. The results, published in the journal Physical Review Letters, move a law-defying "mathematical oddity" ever so slightly up the technology readiness scale

science.title: Too much to do, but too little time? 5 tips to tackle your to-do list
science.summary: With the holidays approaching and the semester winding down, to-do lists are growing. Between shopping for gifts, planning gatherings, studying for finals and finishing projects, there's plenty to accomplish before the end of the year.

science.title: Flowers in Renaissance sculpture may reveal political ambitions of Florence's ruler
science.summary: A new study suggests that the flowers adorning Benvenuto Cellini's sculpture Narcissus are more than decoration: they connect the development of botanical science with competition among Renaissance artists and the ambition of Florence's ruler to consolidate his status.

science.title: Why mega-constellations have a hidden space junk blind spot
science.summary: We are consistently launching more and more stuff into space. As of now, space agencies track more than 30,000 objects larger than a softball, with an expected 1 million more bullet-sized pieces of debris orbiting Earth that are too small to spot from the ground. Government agencies and private commercial entities are planning to have up to 100,000 active spacecraft in orbit by the early 2030s, turning some orbital shells into crowded highways.

science.title: A new reason for magic numbers: Scientists discover the secret behind an unusually stable molecular cluster
science.summary: Why are some groups of molecules remarkably stable while others readily break apart? Researchers at Bar-Ilan University have discovered a surprising explanation for why clusters containing exactly six molecules of glycine, the simplest amino acid, are exceptionally stable—making six a "magic number." Moreover, they have uncovered the reason for this increased stability. The secret lies in a transformation that takes place when the molecules come together: they change their structure and become zwitterions, allowing them to form stronger bonds with one another.

science.title: Mindfulness training may bring out the worst in some employees
science.summary: Contrary to popular belief, mindfulness training in the workplace can make some employees angrier and more likely to treat coworkers with disrespect.

Period. Period!” he emphasized in a phone interview from Brazil with Mongabay. “You may ask […]

environment.summary: The government of Ecuador has approved a new 10-year plan to promote economic activities that make use of the country’s biological resources, while also taking steps to conserve the ecosystems that they rely on. environment.title: Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist
environment.summary: A surprising new study suggests Antarctica's towering ice cliffs may be less vulnerable to catastrophic collapse than scientists once feared. After tracking more than 15,000 ice cliffs, researchers discovered that even the tallest cliffs, which can collapse at alarming speeds, often stabilize rather than triggering an unstoppable chain reaction. Underwater ridges, surrounding water, and broken ice appear to provide natural defenses against further collapse.

environment.title: Scientists discover a surprisingly simple way to turn coffee waste into fuel
environment.summary: Scientists have developed an efficient method to transform used coffee grounds into a potential source of biodiesel while preserving the leftover material for other renewable fuels and valuable chemicals. The discovery could turn millions of tons of discarded coffee waste into a surprisingly useful resource for sustainable energy.

environment.title: DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets
environment.summary: The Shroud of Turin, one of history's most mysterious religious artifacts, is yielding surprising new clues through DNA analysis. Scientists have uncovered a complex mixture of biological traces that may reveal more about the cloth's past and the environments it encountered. The findings offer a fresh scientific perspective on a centuries-old mystery that continues to spark fascination and debate.

environment.title: Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of underwater “marine snow” plays a surprisingly important role in how much carbon reaches the deep ocean. Gooier particles resist bacterial breakdown and can transport more than six times as much carbon to the depths, revealing an unexpected connection between ocean slime and Earth's climate.

environment.title: An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution
environment.summary: A remarkable fossil discovery in Colombia is challenging how scientists understand major evolutionary changes in Earth's history. Researchers uncovered an incredibly diverse ancient marine ecosystem where giant reptiles, sharks, and other creatures thrived as older evolutionary groups approached extinction and newer ones emerged. They call this previously unrecognized pattern a "Biotic Inflection," suggesting that major transformations in life can occur without mass extinctions.

mix_items.title: New EU Bureaucracy Index: EU law has more than doubled since 2010
mix_items.summary: The new EU Bureaucracy Index measures the volume of EU law in force, and it shows a record high: At the end of 2025, the EU regulations and directives in force comprised around 47,600 standard pages, 118% more than in 2010. The volume of EU law has thus more than doubled in 15 years, and it continued to grow in 2025. The main drivers are sanctions regulations and new sets of rules in environmental, consumer and health law.

mix_items.summary: For the first time in more than two decades, the FDA has approved a new hormone therapy for early-stage breast cancer, marking a monumental shift in how the most common form of the disease is treated.

mix_items.title: A star's 'obliquity' likely has little impact on a given planet's habitability
mix_items.summary: A star's axial tilt as it relates to the circumstellar disk that surrounds it is known as stellar obliquity. Over space and time, there are a myriad of solar-type stars with all sorts of obliquities. But the question heretofore has always been what effect a given star's initial obliquity has on the planetary system that forms around it.

mix_items.title: What draws data centers to a community?
mix_items.summary: As Oklahoma communities weigh new data center development, research co-authored by a University of Oklahoma architecture professor offers insight into what draws major technology companies to locations—and why those choices matter locally.

mix_items.title: Hurricane season wrap-up: El Niño fueled record number of Pacific storms but calmed Atlantic
mix_items.summary: The 2026 hurricane season, which officially ends on Nov. 30, will be remembered as a year of contrasts between the Atlantic and Pacific, a classic indication of a hurricane season influenced by a very strong El Niño. Below-normal activity across the Atlantic basin was offset by above-average activity in the Pacific, including two disasters in Hawaii.

mix_items.title: Ultrathin 'rainbow' sails could power spacecraft and shade the Earth
mix_items.summary: For years, whimsically minded space enthusiasts have been dreaming of sailing across the vastness of the void on beams of sunlight. Photons, the massless particles that make up those beams of sunlight, still carry momentum and can therefore impart a gentle push when they bounce off a surface. This force is the concept behind "solar sailing," which has been having a bit of a moment in the last decade as several proof-of-concept flights have shown it is indeed feasible.

mix_items.title: Drones could soon fly blood, defibrillators and medicine to patients
mix_items.summary: Paramedics in one Florida county may soon be able to call in a drone to bring blood to a patient who's bleeding heavily.

mix_items.title: How alfalfa forms root nodules without rhizobia
mix_items.summary: A research team led by professor Feng Jian at the Institute of Genetics and Developmental Biology (IGDB) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences has uncovered a cytokinin–NODULE INCEPTION (NIN) regulatory module associated with spontaneous root nodule formation in alfalfa (Medicago sativa).

mix_items.title: Disrupting a developing brain circuit in adolescence may have lasting social effects
mix_items.summary: Adolescence is often described as a turbulent period of life marked by growing independence, changing social relationships and unpredictable shifts in behavior. According to researchers, tweens' and teens' behavioral changes reflect a brain that is still actively developing, yet scientists know surprisingly little about the neural mechanisms that shape social behavior during this critical stage of life.

mix_items.title: New chemical route delivers first synthesis of plant compound with cough-suppressing potential
mix_items.summary: Neotuberostemonine, a complex plant-derived alkaloid with promising antitussive activity, has remained a challenging target for chemical synthesis for nearly 30 years. Researchers have now achieved its first total synthesis, alongside the synthesis of neostenine and the putative structure of tuberostemonine L. The findings also reveal how the nearly planar geometry of nitrogen atoms contributes to the oxidative instability of these alkaloids, offering new insights and synthetic strategies for natural-product chemistry and future drug discovery.

mix_items.title: England shows widest socioeconomic gap in frailty among 31 countries
mix_items.summary: Older adults from disadvantaged socioeconomic backgrounds experience greater levels of frailty, with England showing the biggest gap between socioeconomic groups among the 31 countries studied.

mix_items.title: Prior authorization limits help expand opioid addiction treatment where approvals were a frequent roadblock, study finds
mix_items.summary: State laws limiting prior authorization requirements for opioid use disorder medications were associated with increased buprenorphine use in Medicaid, but only in states where those requirements were frequent barriers to access, according to a new study led by University of Michigan researchers.

mix_items.title: Laser light reveals where electrons accumulate in atomically thin semiconductor stacks
mix_items.summary: Stacking semiconductors—the chips that power phones, computers and so much more—enables quicker signal movement with less energy, but how does the process actually work? Turns out shining a literal light on the semiconducting materials can help elucidate how the electrons move in the stack, according to a multi-institutional team in Japan. The approach could help inform the development of more efficient, low-power electronics, the researchers said.

mix_items.title: Underwater robots reveal first salp species known to live exclusively in deep sea
mix_items.summary: Salps are barrel-shaped gelatinous animals that play an important role in ocean ecosystems. More than 20 years ago, researchers observed an unfamiliar salp in the deep waters of Monterey Bay. Using specimens and data collected by MBARI's advanced underwater robots, Larry Madin, deputy director emeritus at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution and an MBARI adjunct, recently published a detailed description of the glass salp (Vitreosalpa gemini) in the journal Marine Biodiversity. This striking species is the first salp known to live exclusively in the deep sea.

mix_items.title: FDA approves bezuclastinib in combination with sunitinib as new second-line therapy for patients with GIST
mix_items.summary: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved a combination of bezuclastinib plus sunitinib as second-line therapy after first-line treatment with imatinib for adults with advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) based on evidence from the phase 3 PEAK study led by Dana-Farber Cancer Institute showing that the combination outperformed standard therapy with sunitinib alone.

mix_items.title: New workflow advances programmable chromosome editing in plants
mix_items.summary: A study published in Nature Protocols on Nov. 17 presents a detailed experimental workflow for programmable chromosome manipulation in plants. The platform was developed by a research group led by Gao Caixia at the Institute of Genetics and Developmental Biology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

mix_items.title: Catalysts come alive—electron microscopy reveals the secret dynamic life of nanoparticles
mix_items.summary: University of Nottingham researchers have uncovered hidden nanoscale transformations that could help design cleaner fuels and more efficient catalysts.

mix_items.title: Mitochondria rebranding: Goodbye, powerhouse of the cell. Hello, lungs of the cell?
mix_items.summary: If you remember one thing from high school biology, there's a good chance it's this: Mitochondria are the powerhouse of the cell.

mix_items.title: Reducing or quitting smoking linked to lower risk for developing psoriasis
mix_items.summary: Smoking reduction is associated with a reduced risk for developing psoriasis, including psoriasis vulgaris (PsV) and palmoplantar pustulosis (PPP), according to a research letter published online Nov. 18 in JAMA Dermatology.

mix_items.title: Local protein supply chain keeps nerve cells' mitochondria in check
mix_items.summary: Some tracers used in hospital scans to check what is happening inside a patient's body are so short-lived they must be made on demand on site or rushed in by courier. A new study led by Angelika Harbauer's group at the Max Planck Institute for Biological Intelligence shows that nerve cells use similar strategies to deliver a protein that checks for damage in their mitochondria, the tiny structures that supply energy, balance calcium levels and perform other vital tasks.

mix_items.title: Sex in Britain has changed significantly, especially among young people
mix_items.summary: The sex lives of people in Britain have shifted markedly since 1990, and their sexual and reproductive health needs are substantial and varied, according to the fourth National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal-4). The first five papers from the survey—one of the largest studies of sexual behavior in the world—are published in The Lancet.

mix_items.title: Microplastics in nearly 8 in 10 fish sampled off Oman's Sohar coast
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Sultan Qaboos University detected microplastics in the gills or digestive tracts of 95 of 120 fish sampled off Sohar in the Sea of Oman. Published in Scientific Reports, the study provides a baseline for tracking microplastic pollution in fish along this stretch of Oman's coast.

mix_items.title: Blind sample test reveals how BepiColombo could decode Mercury's mineral makeup
mix_items.summary: An international team of researchers, including scientists from Planetary Science Institute (PSI), has demonstrated that instruments aboard the BepiColombo spacecraft can operate together to identify the minerals that make up Mercury's surface, addressing a longstanding challenge in planetary science. The findings, published in Planetary and Space Science, come as the joint European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) mission entered orbit around Mercury this week.

mix_items.title: FDA approves Nelkarmi for ALK-positive non-small cell lung cancer
mix_items.summary: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has granted approval to Nelkarmi (neladalkib), a kinase inhibitor, for adults with locally advanced or metastatic anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK)-positive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who were previously treated. The approval was granted to Nuvalent and GSK.

mix_items.title: Carbon-rich soil near old oaks does not attract more earthworms, study finds
mix_items.summary: Solitary oaks in traditional Romanian wood pastures create islands of carbon-rich soil around their trunks. However, a research team led by the Universities of Göttingen and Hildesheim found this does not mean more earthworms. In traditional wood pastures in Romania, the topsoil near the trunk held about a third more organic carbon and a quarter more nitrogen than the open grassland, yet earthworm numbers were no higher. As such trees decline across Europe, it is important to understand what they contribute to the soil. The results were published in the journal Agroforestry Systems.

mix_items.title: Common patterns of b/tsDMARD use identified in rheumatoid arthritis
mix_items.summary: Common patterns of biologic and targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (b/tsDMARD) use are seen among patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), and these patterns are associated with underlying genetic associations, according to a study published online Nov. 20 in Arthritis & Rheumatology.

mix_items.title: Self-assembling nanocarriers show promise for delivering CRISPR to tumors and slowing growth
mix_items.summary: A self-assembling supramolecular nanocarrier protects Cas9 RNPs from degradation, enhances systemic delivery and preferential tumor accumulation, and enables pH-responsive intracellular release. Developed by researchers at the Institute of Science Tokyo, this platform achieved a 37.2% indel frequency at the luciferase target locus in HeLa-Luc tumor tissue in mice, compared with 1.5% with free RNPs, and suppressed tumor growth in separate mouse models. These findings support the further development of systemic CRISPR-based cancer therapies.

mix_items.title: How methylmercury impairs forebrain inhibitory circuits and induces abnormal behavior in mice
mix_items.summary: Global efforts have sought to reduce mercury pollution, but methylmercury (MeHg) remains a persistent environmental hazard that bioaccumulates in aquatic food chains. Humans are exposed to MeHg primarily through contaminated seafood. Minamata disease, officially recognized in Japan in 1956, demonstrated the devastating neurological consequences of MeHg poisoning. Since then, researchers have investigated its neurotoxic effects, including sensory, motor and psychiatric symptoms. Despite clinical reports of behavioral disturbances in people affected by MeHg poisoning, the neural circuits underlying these abnormalities remain poorly understood.

mix_items.title: Quantum blueprint maps a practical path to testing unusual entanglement
mix_items.summary: Adrian Del Maestro knows how to engineer a quantum fingerprint. Rick Mukherjee has a gift for tuning atoms. Their combined expertise has taken a theory sketched out on paper and created a pathway for real experiments. The results, published in the journal Physical Review Letters, move a law-defying "mathematical oddity" ever so slightly up the technology readiness scale

mix_items.title: Too much to do, but too little time? 5 tips to tackle your to-do list
mix_items.summary: With the holidays approaching and the semester winding down, to-do lists are growing. Between shopping for gifts, planning gatherings, studying for finals and finishing projects, there's plenty to accomplish before the end of the year.

mix_items.title: Flowers in Renaissance sculpture may reveal political ambitions of Florence's ruler
mix_items.summary: A new study suggests that the flowers adorning Benvenuto Cellini's sculpture Narcissus are more than decoration: they connect the development of botanical science with competition among Renaissance artists and the ambition of Florence's ruler to consolidate his status.

mix_items.title: HIV viral control is necessary but not sufficient for healthy aging
mix_items.summary: Individuals with HIV show signs of faster biological aging compared with people without HIV. In other words, indicators of bodily functions that can be measured in the blood appear more like those of an older individual than those of someone the same age.

mix_items.title: Why mega-constellations have a hidden space junk blind spot
mix_items.summary: We are consistently launching more and more stuff into space. As of now, space agencies track more than 30,000 objects larger than a softball, with an expected 1 million more bullet-sized pieces of debris orbiting Earth that are too small to spot from the ground. Government agencies and private commercial entities are planning to have up to 100,000 active spacecraft in orbit by the early 2030s, turning some orbital shells into crowded highways.

mix_items.title: A new reason for magic numbers: Scientists discover the secret behind an unusually stable molecular cluster
mix_items.summary: Why are some groups of molecules remarkably stable while others readily break apart? Researchers at Bar-Ilan University have discovered a surprising explanation for why clusters containing exactly six molecules of glycine, the simplest amino acid, are exceptionally stable—making six a "magic number." Moreover, they have uncovered the reason for this increased stability. The secret lies in a transformation that takes place when the molecules come together: they change their structure and become zwitterions, allowing them to form stronger bonds with one another.

mix_items.title: Doctors report less burnout in practices they rate as efficient, even during long workweeks
mix_items.summary: When it comes to physician burnout, how you spend your working hours may matter more than how many hours you work.

mix_items.title: Novel metric accurately distinguishes metastasis from an independent primary tumor
mix_items.summary: Research has found that the newly developed Clonal Relatedness Index (CRI) can accurately determine whether tumors in the same patient share a common clonal origin. The findings, detailed in an article appearing in The Journal of Molecular Diagnostics, have important implications for the clinical management of complex cases of cancers of the digestive system and abdominal lining, specifically gastrointestinal, hepatopancreatobiliary and peritoneal carcinomas.

mix_items.title: Mindfulness training may bring out the worst in some employees
mix_items.summary: Contrary to popular belief, mindfulness training in the workplace can make some employees angrier and more likely to treat coworkers with disrespect.

mix_items.title: ‘We don’t want it’: First Nations reject plan to release mining waste into water source
mix_items.summary: Suncor, Canada’s second-largest oil company, wants to release treated wastewater from mining oil in Alberta’s tar sands into a drinking water source for the community of Fort Chipewyan. Investigative reporter Leana Hosea visited the community to learn more. She joins the Mongabay Newscast this week to detail what she found. “This story is not about […]

mix_items.title: How a feminist lens is shaping my climate reporting (commentary)
mix_items.summary: In university, I took a unit called Environmental Journalism, taught by one of my favorite lecturers. I paid enough attention to pass, but certainly not enough to imagine it becoming a beat I would want to report on. I could not picture myself willingly sifting through scientific research papers, trying to understand ribosomes or learning […]

mix_items.title: Clouded tiger cats are notoriously hard to catch. This young researcher caught seven
mix_items.summary: Tadeu de Oliveira, founder and leader of the Tiger Cats Conservation Initiative, a group of scientists committed to studying the smallest wildcats of South and Central America, wanted to be crystal clear: “It is rare to catch a tiger cat. Period. Period!” he emphasized in a phone interview from Brazil with Mongabay. “You may ask […]

mix_items.title: Ecuador’s bioeconomy plan vows sustainability, but faces a test of government priorities
mix_items.summary: The government of Ecuador has approved a new 10-year plan to promote economic activities that make use of the country’s biological resources, while also taking steps to conserve the ecosystems that they rely on. It aims to innovate agribusiness, ecotourism, and other industries in rural areas, without threatening the environment or Indigenous communities. The National […]

mix_items.title: As new season starts, Antarctic krill-fishing vessels face urgent conservation decision (commentary)
mix_items.summary: Despite promising developments, the 27 member states of the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR) have again failed to reach an agreement that protects the Southern Ocean. Mired by consensus decision-making and shrouded from public view by confidentiality rules, Antarctica’s governance systems are no longer fulfilling their mandate. This leaves room […]

mix_items.title: In the Bolivian Andes, Indigenous women plant native trees to restore water sources
mix_items.summary: The bare ridges of the Tunari mountain range rise high in Bolivia’s central Cochabamba department. Only the occasional stand of squat, shrubby trees and rust-red potato crops dot the slopes. It wasn’t always this way. The high-elevation landscape was once filled with native Kewiña (Polylepis sp.) trees, a slow-growing tree belonging to the rose family […]

mix_items.title: Indigenous peoples leave collapsed climate talks with promises on hold
mix_items.summary: ANATALYA, Türkiye — A year ago, a record number of Indigenous people attended the United Nations climate summit in Belém, Brazil. Although there as observers, without a seat at the negotiating table, they left with promises: recognition of their lands, a share of a new forest fund, and a just transition mechanism in the making. […]

mix_items.title: Global marine conservation gathering seeks solutions amid mounting ocean challenges
mix_items.summary: EDINBURGH — Ocean conservation efforts are being hindered by inadequate funding, as well as difficulties translating research into action, according to attendees of an international marine conservation congress in Scotland. Between Nov. 13 and 16, nearly 800 attendees from more than 65 countries convened in the Scottish capital, Edinburgh, for the eighth International Marine Conservation […]

mix_items.title: Indonesia fires test palm oil certification scheme as NGOs question RSPO accountability
mix_items.summary: JAKARTA — Environmental groups are questioning the effectiveness of a global organization that develops standards and certification for sustainable palm oil production after fires affected thousands of hectares in concessions belonging to its members in Indonesia — including areas certified under its sustainability scheme. The criticism came as the organization, the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm […]

mix_items.title: Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle
mix_items.summary: Researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a compound that could transform weight-loss treatment by helping the body burn more energy instead of suppressing appetite like Ozempic and Wegovy. In mice, the compound boosted energy expenditure by up to 18%, improved blood sugar control, reduced liver fat, and promoted weight loss without significant muscle loss. Even more promising, combining it with existing GLP-1 medications produced greater benefits than either treatment alone.

mix_items.title: Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist
mix_items.summary: A surprising new study suggests Antarctica's towering ice cliffs may be less vulnerable to catastrophic collapse than scientists once feared. After tracking more than 15,000 ice cliffs, researchers discovered that even the tallest cliffs, which can collapse at alarming speeds, often stabilize rather than triggering an unstoppable chain reaction. Underwater ridges, surrounding water, and broken ice appear to provide natural defenses against further collapse.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a surprisingly simple way to turn coffee waste into fuel
mix_items.summary: Scientists have developed an efficient method to transform used coffee grounds into a potential source of biodiesel while preserving the leftover material for other renewable fuels and valuable chemicals. The discovery could turn millions of tons of discarded coffee waste into a surprisingly useful resource for sustainable energy.

mix_items.title: DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets
mix_items.summary: The Shroud of Turin, one of history's most mysterious religious artifacts, is yielding surprising new clues through DNA analysis. Scientists have uncovered a complex mixture of biological traces that may reveal more about the cloth's past and the environments it encountered. The findings offer a fresh scientific perspective on a centuries-old mystery that continues to spark fascination and debate.

mix_items.title: Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of underwater “marine snow” plays a surprisingly important role in how much carbon reaches the deep ocean. Gooier particles resist bacterial breakdown and can transport more than six times as much carbon to the depths, revealing an unexpected connection between ocean slime and Earth's climate.

mix_items.title: An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution
mix_items.summary: A remarkable fossil discovery in Colombia is challenging how scientists understand major evolutionary changes in Earth's history. Researchers uncovered an incredibly diverse ancient marine ecosystem where giant reptiles, sharks, and other creatures thrived as older evolutionary groups approached extinction and newer ones emerged. They call this previously unrecognized pattern a "Biotic Inflection," suggesting that major transformations in life can occur without mass extinctions.
